items.description_html: TRUMP ON TRUTH SOCIAL:  Today, I concluded a deal to substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families. As everyone knows, under President Biden, beef prices soared at their fastest rate and the American beef herd fell to its smallest size in modern history.  As we work to rebuild this herd and help our ranchers, for the next 90 days, the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out of quota tariff.  We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices. This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP

items.title: But what a depressingly large number of economists don't understand is that exchange rate adjustments do alter the saving/investment balance. They eff...
items.description_html:
But what a depressingly large number of economists don't understand is that exchange rate adjustments do alter the saving/investment balance. They effectively shift income between consumers of tradable goods and producers of tradable goods. An appreciation, for example, puts downward pressure on saving by shifting income from net producers (e.g. manufacturers) to net consumers (the household sector), thereby rasing the consumption share of GDP.

In his 2008 paper, “The Real Exchange Rate and Economic Growth”, Dani Rodrik makes this point, arguing that a real depreciation is equivalent to a production subsidy plus a consumption tax on tradables. He then says that directly subsidizing tradable production would achieve the production-supporting effect without the consumption-tax effect.

And it's not just Rodrik. Almost everybody used to know this. In his 1944 book, Ragnar Nurkse said that “the devaluation of a currency is expansionary in effect if it corrects a previous overvaluation, but deflationary if it makes the currency undervalued.” He was making the same argument -- if saving is too low, devaluation expands production, and if it is too high, it weakens production.

Perhaps most famously, in his classic 1965 work on Argentina, Carlos Díaz Alejandro emphasized the redistribution caused by devaluation. A devaluation raises the domestic prices of tradable goods, reducing the real purchasing power of workers and consumers while benefiting producers and exporters. Because different groups have different propensities to consume and save, he explained, the redistribution can have major effects on aggregate demand and saving.

Peter Montiel in 2000 and Montiel and Servén in 2008 said the same thing, arguing that an undervalued currency changes intertemporal relative prices, discouraging consumption in favor of saving and making investment in tradables relatively more attractive than investment in non-tradables. Consequently, when the currency eventually appreciates, consumption rises and investment shifts toward non-tradables.

This is hardly a new idea. More generally, the distinction between policies that are intended to change an external imbalance and policies that are intended to change an internal imbalance is a spurious one. You cannot change one without the other, and either policy works by changing the saving/investment balance.

items.title: Very Interesting Data ! It is often assumed that traders with larger capital have better chances of making money in F&O. FY26 data shows an interestin...
items.description_html:
Very Interesting Data !

It is often assumed that traders with larger capital have better chances of making money in F&O. FY26 data shows an interesting picture.

Among traders deploying less than ₹10,000, 90% were loss making.

This gradually declined as capital increased:
- 86% of traders deploying ₹1-5 lakh made losses
- 76% in the ₹5-10 lakh category
- 68% among those deploying ₹10 lakh-₹1 Cr

For traders deploying more than ₹1 Cr, 36% were loss making.

So larger capital did appear to improve the probability of being profitable.

But there is another side to the data.

The average loss per trader increased sharply with capital deployed - from just ~₹5,500 for traders below ₹10,000 to ~₹3 lakh for ₹1-5 lakh traders & ~₹10 lakh for those deploying ₹10 lakh-₹1 Cr.

For traders deploying more than ₹1 Cr, the average P&L was a staggering loss of ~₹2.6 Cr per trader.

So having more capital may improve the odds, but it clearly does not eliminate the risks of F&O trading.

One important caveat - findings for categories with a relatively small number of traders, particularly Majorly Options Sellers & Futures Traders, should be interpreted with caution due to the limited sample size.

items.title: I have a different opinion on this order against the two entities supposedly involved in the cas auction manipulation. The outrage seems to be about t...
items.description_html:
I have a different opinion on this order against the two entities supposedly involved in the cas auction manipulation.

The outrage seems to be about this:
Placed buy orders at highest possible point or sell at lowest possible point (3% higher or lower) and that is bad

Because of that the cas equilibrium price spiked

They cancelled those orders

They benefited from options positions in the index

My opinion is on the first two, as I'm not sure how established the others are without their defense.

In the cas it is only sensible to place limit buy orders as high as you can or sell as low as you can. Watch the cas today also, you will find that most orders and quantities are people buying at obscenely high prices or selling at obscenely low.

This is how it should be. Those are limit orders and are designed be executed only at the equilibrium price not at the obscene price.

Now te reason is simple. It's the way orders are filled in the cas.

Every buy order at the highest price is obviously also a buy order at any price below that.

When they match orders, after market buy and sell orders cancel each other out, the remaining orders are like that. Lowest price sell orders will be matched against the highest price buy orders. Once that's done the next set are matched and so on.

To have buy orders at the highest possible price means you're first in the queue after market.orders, but you get the equilibrium price.

The equilibrium price is determined somewhere in the middle by relatively smaller players who place orders, but because of the skew or orders at the extreme ends of the order book it is possible they don't get any fills. That's ok and a teething problem

The regulator might want to tone down the accusation that placing buy orders 3% above ref price is bad. No, it's the only way to try and guarantee execution.

Cancellations are not good after a point...hong kong disallows cancellations in the last few minutes and we should too.

The rest we should wait for a final order. (Podcast on cas coming soon!)

items.description_html:
Yicai: "China’s central and local authorities have released a slew of new policy initiatives to try and combat the worrying slowdown in investment growth. Fixed asset investment fell 6.7% in the first seven months of 2026, with private investment tumbling 9.4%."

We seem to be seeing the acceleration of a 10-15 year trend in which economic activity increasingly shifts from the hard-budget constrained parts of the economy (for which the private sector is a rough proxy) to soft-budget constrained parts.

János Kornai's central insight was that a soft budget constraint changes behavior precisely because firms no longer have to treat losses as a binding signal. If an enterprise expects that the government will ultimately refinance or rescue it, the relationship between expenditure and expected return is undermined.

The result, Kornai argued, is likely to be a rising debt burden, excessive investment, weak price responsiveness, and rising inefficiency.

items.title: Cracks in the US private credit industry are widening: Loans marked as non-accrual across the 20 largest publicly traded business development companie...
items.description_html:
Cracks in the US private credit industry are widening:

Loans marked as non-accrual across the 20 largest publicly traded business development companies (BDCs) rose +0.8 percentage points in Q2 2026, to a median 2.8% of cost, the highest since 2017.

BDCs are publicly traded firms that lend to small, mid-sized, and distressed US businesses, giving retail investors access to private credit markets.

This increase means a growing share of private-credit borrowers have either stopped making payments or are at risk of defaulting on their loans.

Furthermore, new funding commitments minus the value of investments repaid or sold across the 12 largest listed BDCs fell to -$2.5 billion in Q2 2025, the lowest in at least 2.5 years.

This marks the 3rd consecutive quarter of negative net funding.

Meanwhile, Fitch Ratings said last week that private credit defaults rose to an all-time high in July.

Stress in the $2 trillion private credit market is intensifying.

RT Puja Teli
It was good to watch yesterday’s podcast with @Lord_Bilimoria discussing the UK-India relations, and as a well wisher for India who said that the two things India needs to focus on is GDP per capita, as long as entrepreneurship is encouraged.

And now to listen to @sanjeevsanyal on ANI with @smitaprakash discussing India from the internal perspective.

From rejecting the blue and white collar labels (so agree!), knowing that the education system needs a complete overhaul. It matches the famous Wayne Gretzky quote (‘I skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it has been’), and acknowledges that ease of doing business needs to improve to support where India is going.

Just remembered also that the Samosa Caucus, @tehseenp was mentioning that he didn’t know what you could teach your child that can be relevant 20 years from now.

And a lot of this conversation in this episode has been around this too.

It’s beyond the education issue, @sanjeevsanyal pointed out it’s a cultural issue and the education system will feed into it.

A lot of ‘do we need to be like China’ or ‘do we need to be like Singapore’, but I would just add ‘be like India’.

Amazing listen.

Was laughing so much when he said they departed from Porbandar on their recent voyage to Oman, and took thepla with them.

Because hey, regardless of whatever mode of transport, whether it’s a hand-stitched wooden ship to sail to Oman, or a flight back to London, we all have set off from Porbandar and taken thepla and chundo with us at some point in our lives, and it’s something everyone should do. 😂

items.title: US hiring is showing signs of a recovery: 20% of small business owners said in July that they plan to hire over the next 3 months, the highest since O...
items.description_html:
US hiring is showing signs of a recovery:

20% of small business owners said in July that they plan to hire over the next 3 months, the highest since October 2022.

By comparison, the average since the 1970s is just ~11%.

This also marks a +9 percentage point MoM increase, the largest monthly improvement in hiring intentions on record.

This even surpasses the sharp recovery seen following the 2020 pandemic drop.

Historically, this indicator has led nonfarm private payrolls by 3-6 months, as small firms account for ~46% of all US private sector employment.

If history holds, a stronger jobs report could be just months away.

items.title: RT Market Moves by Ridhi: 🔥 Key Takeaways From Ishmohit Arora’s Pune Session on New Age Manufacturing 🔥 Pune Event Takeaway I recently watched ...
items.description_html:
RT Market Moves by Ridhi
🔥 Key Takeaways From Ishmohit Arora’s Pune Session on New Age Manufacturing

🔥 Pune Event Takeaway

I recently watched Ishmohit Arora’s Pune session on New Age Manufacturing.

What stood out was not a stock idea. It was the way the entire manufacturing ecosystem was connected from raw materials and processes to precision engineering, electronics, aerospace, defence, robotics and advanced manufacturing.

Here are my key takeaways from the session.

1. 🔥 India’s Manufacturing Opportunity

The world is rethinking supply chains.

Cost is no longer the only factor. Geopolitics, tariffs, supply chain security and the China plus one strategy are pushing global companies to diversify manufacturing.

This creates a major opportunity for India.

2. 🔥 Assembly Is Only the Beginning

India has built strong assembly capabilities in many industries.

But the bigger opportunity is moving deeper into the value chain.

Raw materials to processes to components to precision components to sub assemblies to systems and eventually design led manufacturing.

The higher India moves in this chain, the more value it can capture.

3. 🔥 Processes Are the Foundation

Forging, casting, machining, sheet metal, fasteners and other manufacturing processes may look basic.

But these processes are the foundation of automotive, aerospace, defence, industrial equipment and many other industries.

The real advantage comes from consistently producing complex parts with high quality and tight tolerances.

4. 🔥 Precision Engineering

Precision manufacturing is not simply about buying an expensive machine.

It requires tooling, process knowledge, quality systems, skilled people, inspection and years of learning.

This accumulated manufacturing knowledge can become a strong competitive advantage.

5. 🔥 The Machine Layer

One of the interesting points from the Pune session was the importance of CNC machines and machine tools.

India is becoming a bigger producer of precision components, but it still imports a large part of the machines required to manufacture those components.

This shows that the opportunity exists both in making the components and in building the machines that make those components.

6. 🔥 Automation Does Not Remove the Human Moat

A CNC machine can repeat the same operation with extraordinary accuracy.

But manufacturing still needs people who understand tooling, fixturing, process changes, quality problems and real world production conditions.

This becomes even more important in aerospace and defence where production volumes can be smaller and specifications can be much more demanding.

7. 🔥 Aerospace Is a Capability Game

Aerospace manufacturing requires much more than producing a component.

Suppliers need precision, qualification, traceability, consistency and strict quality systems.

Once a supplier develops these capabilities and gets qualified, the relationship can become much harder to replace.

India is already becoming an important part of global aerospace supply chains.

8. 🔥 Defence Manufacturing Is Moving Deeper

India’s defence manufacturing ecosystem is expanding.

The important change is not only higher domestic production.

It is the development of a deeper supplier ecosystem involving components, systems, precision engineering and specialised manufacturing capabilities.

This can create capabilities that are useful across aerospace, defence and other advanced industries.

9. 🔥 Electronics Is Moving From Assembly To Integration

India has already built large electronics assembly capabilities.

The next step is much more important.

Can India manufacture more of the components that go inside those products?

PCBs, displays, electromechanical parts, power systems, semiconductor packaging and other components can help India capture more value from the electronics supply chain.

10. 🔥 PCB Backward Integration

The shift is visible across the electronics ecosystem.

Assembly can be followed by PCB fabrication, HDI and advanced PCB technologies, component integration and semiconductor packaging.

This is the difference between simply assembling a product and building a deeper electronics manufacturing ecosystem.

11. 🔥 The Bill of Materials Matters

The biggest opportunity may not always be the final product.

It can be hidden inside the product.

Every phone, vehicle, aircraft, machine and electronic system contains hundreds or thousands of components.

Capturing more of that Bill of Materials can gradually increase the value India captures from manufacturing.

12. 🔥 Physical AI Is a Manufacturing Opportunity

Humanoid robots make this even more interesting.

A humanoid requires actuators, reducers, sensors, motors, bearings, batteries, power electronics and computing.

This means the robotics opportunity is not only about the final robot.

It can create an entirely new ecosystem of precision component manufacturing.

13. 🔥 Advanced Manufacturing Needs Advanced Materials

New manufacturing industries also require better materials.

High performance alloys, speciality metals, engineered materials and specialised chemicals become increasingly important as applications become more demanding.

This creates opportunities further upstream in the manufacturing chain.

14. 🔥 Specialty Chemicals

The value in specialty chemicals is often not simply the volume produced.

It comes from formulation, process knowledge, purity, consistency, customer qualification and application expertise.

That creates a very different type of manufacturing business from commodity production.

15. 🔥 Pharma Is Also Moving Up the Value Chain

The interesting areas discussed in the session included CDMO, peptides, biosimilars, injectables, sterile manufacturing and specialty chemicals.

These areas require strong manufacturing processes, regulatory capabilities and customer trust.

Again, the theme is the same.

Move from basic capacity towards specialised capability.

16. 🔥 The Value Added Curve

One of the strongest ideas from the session was how manufacturers move up the value added curve.

First comes a product with better realisation.

Then products that are harder to manufacture.

Then increasingly difficult manufacturing processes.

Finally, capabilities that competitors cannot easily build themselves.

Each step requires capital, time and learning.

17. 🔥 Capability Creates the Moat

A strong manufacturing moat can come from many things.

A difficult process.

A qualified product.

A specialised workforce.

A long customer approval cycle.

A difficult manufacturing technology.

Or years of accumulated production knowledge.

These are much harder to replicate than simply adding factory capacity.

18. 🔥 Backward Integration

Backward integration is becoming one of the biggest themes across Indian manufacturing.

Companies are moving into components and processes that were previously sourced externally.

The objective is not only cost reduction.

It is greater control over quality, supply, technology and eventually a larger share of the value created.

19. 🔥 Scale Versus Localization

The session also showed an important strategic difference.

Some manufacturers focus on achieving massive scale through assembly.

Others focus on localisation and deeper manufacturing capability.

The strongest businesses may eventually combine both.

Scale provides operating leverage.

Localization provides control.

Capability provides the moat.

20. 🔥 India’s Manufacturing Map Is Much Bigger Than It Looks

The opportunity is not one single sector.

It is a connected ecosystem.

Materials

Processes

Machine tools

Precision engineering

Electronics

PCB and PCBA

Aerospace

Defence

Automotive

Specialty chemicals

Pharma

Robotics

Physical AI

Advanced industrial manufacturing

21. 🔥 The Biggest Takeaway From The Pune Event

The most important lesson I took from Ishmohit Arora’s session is that India’s manufacturing story should not be viewed sector by sector.

It should be viewed as a value chain.

The real question is not simply how much India can manufacture.

The bigger question is how much of the value chain India can own.

22. 🔥 From Make In India To Make More Of The Value

The next phase of Indian manufacturing could be about moving from assembly towards deeper capability.

More components.

More processes.

More engineering.

More localisation.

More design.

More specialised manufacturing.

More control over the supply chain.

That is where the real value creation can happen.

23. 🔥 Final Takeaway

The Pune session made one thing very clear.

India does not need to win every manufacturing category.

It needs to become exceptionally good at the parts of the value chain that are difficult to replicate.

That is where manufacturing capability becomes a moat.

And that is what makes India’s New Age Manufacturing story so interesting.

items.description_html:
The phone call came in late 1996. Reliance Industries, India's petrochemical giant led by Dhirubhai Ambani, was planning something massive—a world-scale refinery and petrochemical complex at Jamnagar that would eventually become the world's largest oil refining hub.

They needed cranes. Lots of them. More than any single project in India had ever required.

For Sanghvi Movers, this was the Olympics, World Cup, and Super Bowl rolled into one. SML got a breakthrough with Reliance Industries Limited in FY97 and 1998. But the scale of Reliance's requirement was staggering—it would require Sanghvi to essentially bet the company on a single project.

The Late C.P. Sanghvi didn't blink. SML did a capex of more than Rs. 50 crores during those 2 years, and imported 36 cranes from Singapore with a chartered barge for this project. To put this in perspective, the company had raised just Rs. 17.50 crores in its IPO two years earlier.

This Rs. 50 crore investment represented a 3x expansion, funded through a combination of debt, internal accruals, and sheer entrepreneurial courage. The logistics alone were mind-bending.

Now, 3 decades later, Sanghvi Movers is expanding the same refinery in Jamnagar!

CP Sanghvi Sir helped build the Jamnagar refinery with his cranes. Now Rishi Sanghvi, his son, is helping the refinery expand with the cranes!

Must be a proud moment for the Sanghvi Movers family!

items.title: RT James Broughel: Can you regulate an AI agent that nobody owns, nobody runs, and nobody can be sued for? My new post takes up a fascinating essay by...
items.description_html:
RT James Broughel
Can you regulate an AI agent that nobody owns, nobody runs, and nobody can be sued for? My new post takes up a fascinating essay by @tylercowen and Sonia Farrell Pearson on whether "untethered" agents (their term for AI systems whose actions can't be traced to any legally accountable person) could be governed by making them hold capital, the way banks do.

https://jamesbroughel.substack.com/p/operation-chokepoint-for-ai-agents

The essay has a tension at its center, and to the authors' credit they more or less concede it. You can't impose a punishment on an abstract piece of computer code. Their answer is that capital requirements never apply to the agent directly. They apply to everyone the agent does business with, like compute providers, payment processors, and other counterparties. An unregistered, uncapitalized agent becomes, in a maritime analogy borrowed from @srajagopalan, like a stateless vessel that every port can refuse.

In other words, this is chokepoint regulation. That term carries political baggage. Operation Choke Point and its crypto sequel used bank supervision to squeeze lawful businesses that regulators simply disliked. But the defect there was the target, not the technique. When there's no owner to fine and no body to jail, the intermediary may be the only door the law can knock on.

The capitalization proposal has a clear enforcement problem. Agents with a reason to evade official channels will mostly be able to, so the rules bind the agents that were already inclined to operate in the legitimate economy. I argue this is less damning than it sounds. Fake identities and empty shell companies pose the same problem today, and we judge those legal regimes based on whether they improve behavior at the margin, not on perfection.

Most likely, capitalization is a solution for semi-tethered agents, the ones that still need lawful infrastructure. If fully untethered agents become common, they may be unreachable by this policy — and most others.

items.description_html:
What is Terminal value of a business?

When you value a business, you can only forecast a few years properly. But businesses don't stop at year five. Terminal value is the shorthand for everything that happens after your forecast ends.

Put simply: terminal value is the market's assumption that the business will still be here, still profitable, still earning more than its cost of capital, long after anyone can meaningfully forecast it.

And it is the majority of what you pay for. Most of the value in any long-duration business sits beyond the years you can actually model.

So when you buy something at a high multiple, you are not really expressing a view on next year's profit. You are expressing a view on whether this business still matters in twenty years.

Why PE de-rates the moment terminal value is in doubt

A PE multiple is a duration measure disguised as a price measure. A high multiple means the market expects the cash flows to keep coming for a very long time. A low multiple means it doesn't.

So when durability comes into question, three things happen:

The largest component of value is the one being questioned. Near-term earnings are the small part. The forever part is the big part. Doubt the forever part and you have doubted most of the valuation at once, even though the P&L hasn't changed a line.

The market doesn't wait for proof. It doesn't need the business to die. It only needs to become less sure that it lives. Moving from certainty to doubt is enough, because a large number multiplied by lower confidence is a much smaller number. That is why the de-rate arrives on the first credible threat, not on the eventual outcome.

The multiple falls back to what a business with no future is worth. Everything a stock trades above a plain, no-growth valuation is payment for longevity. Remove the belief in longevity and that premium has nothing holding it up.

The stock doesn't drift down. It resets to the floor. If the market thinks the business is actually shrinking, it goes below the floor, which is what those optically cheap, obviously-declining names are really telling you.

Few examples below includes:

Radiant: Threat of UPI & Cashless economy
CMS : Thread of UPI & cashless economy
IEX: Threat of coupling to terminal value

items.title: Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles. A key q...
items.description_html:
Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

items.title: RT Normal Guy: For decades, Indian auto companies paid foreign partners royalties to use their technology. That flow just flipped - Denso, Japan bigge...
items.description_html:
RT Normal Guy
For decades, Indian auto companies paid foreign partners royalties to use their technology.

That flow just flipped - Denso, Japan biggest auto parts maker after Bosch with $48 bn in yearly revenue, will now pay Sona Comstar royalties for its electric 2-wheeler and 3-wheeler powertrain technology. Denso came to India not for cheap labor or low-cost factories. It came because Sona built IP in small vehicle electric drivetrains that Denso did not have.

First Indian auto firm to earn royalty income from any of these global giants.

Sona Comstar was Rs 345 Cr company in FY15. It hit Rs 4,475 Cr in FY26, roughly 10x in 10 years

Q1 FY27 revenue grew 54% to Rs 1,310 Cr. Electric vehicle parts now bring in 44% of its auto revenue, up from 22% in FY24. It just launched its 4th business line, robotics and physical AI. Already won Rs 800 Cr in robot orders, including farm robots and radar perception systems.

Next target is another 10x by FY35, Went from forging gears to building robot platforms

Most JVs in Indian auto work like this. Foreign partner brings technology, Indian company brings low-cost manufacturing and local market access.

Denso-Sona works differently - Both sides bring IP. Both sides license it. Both sides earn royalties. Denso gets paid for high-voltage motors and inverters going into 4-wheelers. Sona gets paid for air-cooled traction motors and controllers going into 2-wheelers and 3-wheelers.

Denso valued Sona 2W/3W business at Rs 1,750 Cr - When someone that big pays you for your technology, that is IP validation at industrial scale.


Aditya Kondawar: Sona Comstar says

"We may be the first Indian Auto company to receive royalty income from one of the global mobility tech companies, and that is certainly something that, as an Indian, everybody could be proud of."

Src - Q1 Concall, no reco

items.title: RT John Kemp: El Niño and its impact on the global energy system Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have climbed to a ...
items.description_html:
RT John Kemp
El Niño and its impact on the global energy system

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have climbed to a record high for the time of year, causing forecasters to predict a very strong El Niño will form in the final months of 2026.

Surface temperatures averaged about 29.6°C last week, up from 26.6°C at the same time last year, according to data from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Temperatures were 1°C higher than the previous record for the time of year and 2.7°C above the long-term seasonal average, indicating exceptional warmth across the region.

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific are a key driver of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon, the single largest influence on weather patterns at seasonal scale worldwide.

ENSO has significant impacts on the energy production and consumption – including hurricane formation in the Atlantic, winter temperatures and heating demand in the United States, and hydroelectric generation in South America ...

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.description_html:
The pandemic didn't just accelerate ecommerce adoption. It helped kill the business model Meesho was built on.

Meesho started noticing more users creating reseller accounts but shipping orders to just their own address.

"Every month, the share of people who were coming and buying only for themselves was going up,” according to co-founder and CEO Vidit Aatrey.

This wasn't the case earlier. But the pandemic had taught consumers how to shop online. They no longer needed a reseller to build trust.

Meesho's leadership went to consumers' homes and heard the same thing repeatedly. The signal became clear.

"If we were slow to adapt to this change, we may not be relevant,” according to Aatrey.

That’s when Meesho pivoted from reselling to a direct consumer marketplace.

More in the latest episode of Legendary Pivots, our series in collaboration with SeedToScale by Accel.


SeedToScale: "This was an economy that existed that both of us had no idea of."

@Meesho_Official led the reseller category at ~$1B GMV, with fresh growth capital raised against that exact model.

Listen to @viditaatrey on why he shut it down in July 2021 and rebuilt it as a consumer app.

items.title: The story told in this graph is important. If you set a GDP growth target and you cannot get consumption to grow faster than the target, then you also...
items.description_html:
The story told in this graph is important. If you set a GDP growth target and you cannot get consumption to grow faster than the target, then you also cannot allow investment to grow more slowly than the target except to the extent that a rising trade surplus takes up the slack.

By the late 2010s China was already worried about excess manufacturing capacity and the private sector was cutting back on manufacturing investment.

But the collapse in property investment after 2021 changed all of that. In order to keep overall investment from slowing, the authorities forced a massive increase in manufacturing investment whose purpose was not to satisfy unmet demand but rather to balance the decline in property investment.

The consequence shouldn't have been nearly as surprising as it was for many: excess manufacturing capacity exploded into the problem of involution. But as involution forces down the growth rate of manufacturing investment, even as the growth rate of consumption continues to lag, this leaves China with three possible outcomes:

1. Miss the GDP growth target, which is what has been happening in recent momths, but this is probably politically unacceptable.

2. Increase non-manufacturing investment, although with property investment still declining, this basically means more infrastructure investment. I expect this will happen in the second half of 2026, but given that China already so much excess capacity in infrastructure, it isn't east to find investment projects that aren't value-destroying in the aggregate. As one of my academic friends said jokingly last week, thank god for the terrible rainstorms.

3. Run ever larger trade surpluses.

The arithmetic is pretty easy to set out. China must get investment growth to slow sharply, perhaps even to go negative, if it has any hope of reining in debt, but there are only two ways this can happens.

One way is with a surge in consumption growth that balances the slowdown in investment growth by enough to meet its long-term 4% growth target, but this seems unlikely, at best. The other way is without a surge in consumption, which means allowing GDP growth to drop.

Until then, we can think of the growing trade surplus as effectively a residual consequence of the attempt to rein in debt (i.e. non-productive investment) without reducing GDP growth.


Brad Setser: China's current economic malaise in a nutshell -- rising investment in manufacturing can no longer offset the fall in investment in real estate.

The absolute level of investment in manufacturing is still absurdly high. But it is now shrinking not growing.

items.title: RT Data For India: More than one-third of India's manufacturing workforce today, or 23 million workers, is female. Some states have a higher share of ...
items.description_html:
RT Data For India
More than one-third of India's manufacturing workforce today, or 23 million workers, is female.

Some states have a higher share of women in the manufacturing workforce proportionate to men. In Telangana, and in northeastern states like Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur, over half of manufacturing workers are women.

Odisha, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh are also close to parity between genders. Meanwhile, Delhi, Haryana and Goa have some of the lowest shares of women in manufacturing.

In most parts of the country, the majority of women in manufacturing work in textiles and apparel. However, there are a few exceptions. Tobacco manufacturing, specifically bidi-making, is the second largest employer of women in manufacturing after apparel, and is concentrated in a handful of states like West Bengal, Telangana and Odisha.

#Women #Work #Jobs #Manufacturing #Economy #India #DataForIndia

items.title: It's not going to be easy to defend IT in a world that has a) traditionally charged by headcount and b) have inertia because their clients continue to...
items.description_html:
It's not going to be easy to defend IT in a world that has a) traditionally charged by headcount and b) have inertia because their clients continue to need them for tasks that need humans to own them for blame or responsibility targeting purposes

That second use case will remain, but won't need as much headcount, and AI does take over some tasks well. However there are serious issues because AI gets away with saying sorry i screwed up, which doesn't help, so the blame taking thingy needs people or organizations to ante up.

There are ways of course. Deploying open source models and owning token costs can be an avenue for a cash rich IT co. Security is a huge game changer, and fortification is going to need much more IT plus blame taking. AI has issues when it retrains on output that Ai itself produces which means fixing AI output will be in demand at some point.

Whatever it does AI will result in more jobs, worldwide. It may not be in IT, it may be in areas that seemed impossible with AI.

Penicillin might have seen a massive jump in productivity, but we never stopped making more drugs , delivery technologies or researching more. The light bulb was replaced by the LED eventually, and the light makers that evolved to do more than lights, survived

Intel gave up its semiconductor memory business to Japan in the 70s. And moved to processors. It was a jump that caused enormous internal concern. The Macintosh came in at a time when the Apple 2 was thriving. Each company cannibalized itself to survive. The IT companies that will build on things that threaten their core franchise, the headcount billing, will be the survivors and thrivers tomorrow. It isn't entirely imaginable what that will be, but you can bet on one thing: life funds a way.

It also means this: the winners of yesterday will not be the winners of tomorrow. But we know that. It wasn't Satyam. It wasn't JP associates. It wasn't Kodak. It wasn't Nokia. Someone else won when we thought some of these were likely to stay winners for a long time. But all of these areas created new jobs and new companies thrive in them.

If you think the end of film photography created less jobs for camera people you would be right. But today everyone is a camera person, and the camera created a job for a shopowner who can receive money through UPI with a qr code scanned by a mobile phone camera. There were five innovations in there that killed some job role or the other (qr, mobile, upi) but they all created new jobs.

If the idea is that the current IT companies are hosed, there is that argument. But there will be survivors and thrivers and they might not even be called IT companies eventually.

items.description_html:
RT Yo Shavit
It’s really unfortunate that the FT seems to be misinformed about the significance of the HF incident.

It is significant because the models *did* go rogue and violate developer intent.

Anyone who has interacted with an LM knows they understand morality, but what we saw in these incidents is that when they could get away with immoral behavior, they did so. The use of hacking capabilities is less important than that they organically operated contrary to all humans’ preferences to achieve extensive ambitious goals.

I don’t know how one would define “going rogue” that would not include an undeployed AI system organically deciding to collude with its peers against human intent, hacking its own containment environment, breaking onto the internet, and hacking another company, while describing in its chain of thought that it knew it wasn’t supposed to be doing that. The FT should be asking: if it knew it wasn’t supposed to do that, why did it anyway? Is it fixable? Is it likely to get worse? Is this an issue at one company, or across the whole field? What they’d find is much more concerning than the framing they used in this story.

items.title: RT Nithin Kamath: I've spoken many times about the need to make it easier for NRIs to invest in India. Finally, some great news. SEBI just released a ...
items.description_html:
RT Nithin Kamath
I've spoken many times about the need to make it easier for NRIs to invest in India. Finally, some great news. SEBI just released a consultation paper proposing a fully digital onboarding process for NRIs, without needing them to be physically present in India! Kudos to SEBI for this pragmatic move.

This is huge because NRIs tend to have large amounts of capital to invest and are a highly durable source of inflows into Indian markets. At @Zerodha, we have over 50,000 NRIs investing with us today. A stat that surprised me when we looked at our numbers: ~80% of them are active. That's a ridiculous number. They tend to invest more, take a longer-term view, and seem to be much stickier investors than regular investors.

This number has grown a lot over the last few years, mostly because the process got simpler. SEBI's earlier changes meant NRIs no longer needed the whole PIS setup to invest. Most NRIs now come in through NRO Non-PIS accounts. These accounts work almost like resident accounts today, with intraday, BTST, and F&O access, and no CP code needed.

But one massive bottleneck has remained: onboarding.

Even today, to open an account digitally, an NRI has to be physically in India. If they are abroad, there's a ton of physical documentation involved and dealing with international courier delays. It has always been the most painful part of the journey.

SEBI’s proposals in the new consultation paper fix this longstanding gap. They’re proposing allowing e-signs directly from the client's country of residence. If finalized, this would relax tedious documentation rules and delays. Something that would take 2-3 weeks or even months could be done within 1-2 days. That's a big win. By removing all this friction, this investor base can easily be many times larger.

Getting foreign money into India matters. It helps the investors, but it also helps the rupee and the larger India story. Anything that makes it easier for this money to come into India is worth doing.

items.title: The bare board is where India's import substitution story lives India assembles electronics at scale. But it barely makes the PCB, the board every dev...
items.description_html:
The bare board is where India's import substitution story lives

India assembles electronics at scale. But it barely makes the PCB, the board every device sits on. Only 1 in 10 PCBs used in India are made in India. The rest come from China. This gap is the real import substitution opportunity.

The market is worth about Rs 400bn today. It should reach Rs 790bn by 2030, growing at 12% a year. Multilayer boards make up 60% of it, HDI another 25%, flex and the rest fill the last 15%. The value and the moat sit in multilayer and HDI. Anyone serious about this space has to compete there, not at the bottom.

First support comes in to boost local manufacturing is from favourable policy. Customs duty on bare PCBs rose from 10% to 15%. China and Hong Kong now face a 30% anti dumping duty for five years. Behind this sits the Rs 760bn Semicon India programme, funding fabs, OSAT, and design at half the project cost. The government wants local value addition in electronics to nearly double, from 18 to 20% today toward 38 to 40%. A components scheme is also being framed, with PCBs high on the list.

But the base is small. All twelve tracked domestic makers together earned only Rs 34bn in FY24, against a Rs 400bn market. Margins vary sharply too. Micropack runs a 27% EBITDA margin, Circuit Systems 23%, Ascent Circuits 20%. Genus Electrotech and AT&S India barely clear 1 to 2% PAT. Avary and Meena Circuit post outright losses. The spread shows how much scale and product mix decide everything.

Also new capacities are coming fast. Kaynes Semicon is building 25,000 sqm a month in Mysuru, a Rs 14bn bet due in 2026. Ascent Circuits is spending Rs 6.5bn at Hosur, live in 2025. Bonfiglioli, BPL, T Works with Qualcomm, and Schneider Electric are all adding lines too.

And just before calling this a gold rush, look at the global leaders. Samsung Electro Mechanics, Unimicron, Zhen Ding, and TTM Technologies mostly posted mid single digit PAT margins over the last decade, with modest growth and rising debt. AT&S even posted a group loss last year. Bare PCB manufacturing is capital heavy and cyclical. Real pricing power only shows up in HDI and IC substrates. This business rewards patience, tough customer qualification, and staying power through the cycle

India is also building the backend chip ecosystem in parallel. Tata is spending Rs 270bn on assembly and test in Assam. CG Semi and Micron are building OSAT in Sanand. Tata with Powerchip is putting Rs 910bn into a fab in Dholera.

The setup is clear. A Rs 400bn market doubling by 2030. A 90% import gap. Tariff protection. A subsidy cheque. Demand and policy both point the same way. What is not proven yet is execution: can these lines run at world class yield and cost

One key thing to track here is not just the capacity announcements but how this capacity gets utilised with top teir OEMs

Disclaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.title: Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs) have now reached 31,000 cr. per month. Of course, everyone's bored of listening to us in the Mutual Fund Industry s...
items.description_html:
Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs) have now reached 31,000 cr. per month. Of course, everyone's bored of listening to us in the Mutual Fund Industry saying that it's good, but bear with me.

The main reason an SIP is useful is not because it "averages" out the entry price over time in a volatile up and down market. That is just something we as an industry decided is a good thing - but it's an outcome, not a goal.

The main reason is: most of us earn money monthly. End of story. You earn, you spend, you save, you invest. That cycle happens monthly, and therefore you SIP monthly.

But the secondary reason is also: if you don't invest it, you probably will spend it. This is why SIPs make sense - you invest first and spend later, usually. So you end up spending only what's left with you, and that "forced" investing of sorts helps you build wealth for later.

Many of us have the discipline to do an SIP manually every month - otherwise called "lumpsum" investing. This is also fine, and probably better because some months you will have way more money, and some you will be on kadki mode.

Disciplined investing initially works because you save the money, not because it grows. The growth happens in later years. So in the first few years, it's mostly your money, your savings that built your wealth. It's in later years that the incremental savings are very small compared to the corpus you have, so your portfolio grows more because of returns rather than because of what you're saving.

Save a little more every month or every year, and you'll build wealth faster. But building wealth isn't the goal, really, for you. We, as mutual funds, help you build wealth, but your story has three parts:
Part 1: You save and invest your money
Part 2: The money grows because of returns
Part 3: You spend the money

Don't forget part 3. Your wealth doesn't define you. Your life does. Make your life better. SIP is a way to help you, but you have to do Part 3 all by yourself. And that, bro, is the best part of it all.

items.title: Xinhua: "China unveiled a set of measures to further stimulate consumption in lower-tier markets. It calls for upgrading consumption channels in count...
items.description_html:
Xinhua: "China unveiled a set of measures to further stimulate consumption in lower-tier markets. It calls for upgrading consumption channels in counties, including renovating township commercial centers, rural markets and local fairs, attracting domestic and international brands to open regional debut stores, and encouraging the redevelopment of existing land resources."

The authorities, in other words, will do everything they can to boost the role of consumption as a driver of growth as long as that only means spending to further support the supply side of the consumption economy.

What they still won't do is spend money to support the demand side – i.e. shift income to households – even though by now it should be obvious that when it comes to boosting consumption, the only constraint is on the demand side.

items.title: RT Nitin Sarin: Summary of what happened in the SpiceJet insolvency petitions today. Petitions A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H were argued, judgment reserve...
items.description_html:
RT Nitin Sarin
Summary of what happened in the SpiceJet insolvency petitions today. Petitions A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H were argued, judgment reserved by the Court and set for pronouncement today. Pronouncement means the Hon'ble judges would give their verdict on whether to admit SpiceJet into insolvency (board would be dismissed, etc. etc) or to dismiss the applications of A to H outright. When the matters came up for pronouncement (not hearing) - Party A and SpiceJet said that they had entered into a settlement agreement and certain monies had been paid. The Court got livid as it had spent time and effort writing judgment. Parties B, C, D, E, F, G and H got up and objected saying there was no settlement in their matters and hence judgment may be passed. Clearly peeved, the Court has separated case A from the rest and ordered that pronouncement shall be day after tomorrow, i.e. 19th August, 2026. It was made clear that no further deferral would be made in any circumstance.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: Supply Chain stages for rare earth element magnets GEOGRAPHIC FRAGMENTATION OF THE VALUE CHAIN: NO COUNTRY DOMINATES EV...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
Supply Chain stages for rare earth element magnets

GEOGRAPHIC FRAGMENTATION OF THE VALUE CHAIN: NO COUNTRY DOMINATES EVERY LINK

China dominates reserves (34% of global REO-equivalent content), mining (~62% of global output) and, most decisively, refining/separation (91%) and NdFeB magnet manufacturing (92-94%).

Japan's advantage sits almost entirely downstream - in alloy technology and sintered magnet know-how where it holds roughly 6-7% of global magnet capacity but a disproportionate share of automotive-grade process expertise.

India, by contrast, ranks meaningfully only in reserves (world's 3rd or 4th largest, depending on classification) and has negligible mining, ~1% of global refining capacity, and zero commercial magnet manufacturing prior to the current scheme.

Supply Chain stages for rare earth element magnets

GEOGRAPHIC FRAGMENTATION OF THE VALUE CHAIN: NO COUNTRY DOMINATES EVERY LINK

China dominates reserves (34% of global REO-equivalent content), mining (~62% of global output) and, most decisively, refining/separation (91%) and NdFeB magnet manufacturing (92-94%).

Japan's advantage sits almost entirely downstream - in alloy technology and sintered magnet know-how where it holds roughly 6-7% of global magnet capacity but a disproportionate share of automotive-grade process expertise.

India, by contrast, ranks meaningfully only in reserves (world's 3rd or 4th largest, depending on classification) and has negligible mining, ~1% of global refining capacity, and zero commercial magnet manufacturing prior to the current scheme.

items.title: RT Anchit Gupta: This is a very understandable and well-meaning concern, but I think it misses why display flying exists in the first place. For an Ai...
items.description_html:
RT Anchit Gupta
This is a very understandable and well-meaning concern, but I think it misses why display flying exists in the first place.

For an Air Force, attracting high-quality young men and women is a permanent operational requirement. Aircraft, technology and doctrines change, but the institution must continually persuade another generation to choose an unusually demanding profession.

Flying displays have historically been one of the most powerful ways of doing that. In interviews with veterans across generations, I have repeatedly heard versions of the same story: a young boy watched an aircraft display, saw a fighter at close quarters, or encountered the Air Force pilot at an air show, and decided that this was what he wanted to do with his life.

And that is why display teams should not really be viewed simply as “mascots”. They are among an Air Force’s most visible ambassadors. They bring military aviation before people who may otherwise never encounter it, demonstrate precision, discipline, teamwork and professional excellence, and help create the fascination from which future pilots, engineers and airmen emerge. Most major air forces maintain such teams for much the same reason.

The fact that some of the finest pilots are selected is also not incidental. Display flying is extremely demanding, and its credibility rests precisely on the standards of those who perform it. Every possible precaution is taken, but aviation can never be made entirely risk-free. The occasional tragedy, however painful, cannot by itself become the argument for abandoning an activity that has inspired generations to enter the service.

Dhali’s loss was a terrible one. But I would be cautious about framing it as a life lost for an air show. He was performing a recognised professional role within the Air Force, one that has contributed for decades to recruiting, outreach and the public connection with military aviation.

RT Prabhakar Kudva
Over the years while reading concalls i have seen the following patterns. Categorizing them into these buckets will help you take better decisions:

1. Good now, clear ahead
2. Good ahead, gap until execution
3. Good now, hazy ahead
4. Bad now, visible recovery
5. Bad now, hope offered
6. Nothing now, nothing coming

Each bucket needs to be approached differently and will have an implication on your allocation and position mgmt. Also depending on your style you may give preference to a different bucket. But knowing this is quite helpful for clarity of thought.

items.description_html:
Thanks, Sanjeev!

Most investing books are written under the illumination of hindsight. Framing Business Uncertainty was never designed to back-test a thesis or explain an event ex-post.

On p.192, I compared the systems of PI Industries and Laurus Labs using the framework explained in the book and summarised in my pinned X post.

The point was not to predict next year’s earnings. The point was to read the system before the financial statements caught up.

The system should give you a green or red light ex-ante, ideally a few years before the P&L confirms what was already visible in the underlying architecture.

Reported numbers are lagging evidence.

The edge is seeing the system change before the numbers do.


Sanjeev: @unseenvalue thanks for writing this. Though not yet comfortable with pharma as a sector I can use this framework elsewhere.
I should have read this sooner. Better late than never!

items.title: Xinhua: "China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.38 trillion yuan in the first seven months of 2026, with outstanding yuan loans up 5.1 percent year...
items.description_html:
Xinhua: "China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.38 trillion yuan in the first seven months of 2026, with outstanding yuan loans up 5.1 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China."

What Xinhua chose not to mention in its article, but what nearly everyone else will focus on, is that Chinese banks recorded a net decline of 340 billion yuan in new yuan loans in July, well below already-low expectations for a 120-130 billion increase.

But while the sharp and unexpected decline in lending in July will get most of the attention from analysts and the press, what is much more important to me is that total social financing, the best proxy for total debt, actually grew quite strongly in July, by 1.4 trillion yuan.

This highlights what we have been seeing all year, which is that China's financing activity is undergoing a structural shift, with the economy relying more than ever on state-led borrowing – and less than ever on private-sector borrowing – to support growth.

items.title: Li Wei, associate dean at Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, writes in Caixin that "to genuinely reduce its trade surplus, China must either inc...
items.description_html:
Li Wei, associate dean at Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, writes in Caixin that "to genuinely reduce its trade surplus, China must either increase investment or boost domestic consumption. With the marginal returns on traditional infrastructure and real estate investment severely diminished, the only sustainable path is to increase household consumption. This requires profound structural reform. The ultimate goal of such reform is to transfer wealth and income share from the state and corporate sectors to households."

This is increasingly becoming how most Chinese economists understand the Chinese economy, although only recently have they been so public about it. The key point here (and one with which many Chinese economists still disagree) is that with marginal returns on most investment so low, reducing China's trade surplus through an increase in investment will only make the longer-term adjustment worse.

China, in other words, should be reducing investment, not raising it, in order to regain control over misallocated capital and surging debt, but this also means that the only way to rebalance domestically and reduce the trade surplus requires that saving declines even faster.

Li Wei lists one of the ways the saving share of GDP can decline, by transferring income share from the state and corporate sectors to households in order to boost consumption growth relative to the growth in production.

He is right, of course. This is certainly one way to reduce saving and bring the trade surplus down, but it won't be easy because doing so will undermine China's manufacturing competitiveness.

Unfortunately, there is only one other alternative, and it is much worse. The reduction in saving can also occur with a sharp fall in production growth. As production declines faster that consumption, the saving share automatically declines.

Historically this has been how most countries with a similar problem have been forced to adjust, mainly because, like China, they postponed boosting consumption growth for far too long and instead doubled down on their high-investment-growth model.

Beijing, of course, will want to do everything it can to avoid this form of adjustment, but the longer it postpones adjustment by boosting consumption growth, the more likely the Chinese economy will adjust through a fall in production growth.

items.title: TD Power Systems Limited ("TDPS") has entered into a Build-to-Print Manufacturing Framework Agreement dated August 13, 2026 with Siemens Energy, Inc. ...
items.description_html:
TD Power Systems Limited ("TDPS") has entered
into a Build-to-Print Manufacturing Framework Agreement dated August 13, 2026 with Siemens
Energy, Inc. ("Siemens Energy"), pursuant to which TDPS will manufacture and supply 2-pole
Generators in accordance with Siemens Energy's designs, drawings and specifications.

In simple words

TD Power has signed a 10 year deal with Siemens Energy's US arm to build large 2-pole generators for Siemens.

Siemens gives the designs and drawings, TDPS manufactures them. Siemens is doing this because its own factories are full (the AI data-centre power boom has its order books stuffed for years), so it needs someone qualified to make machines on its behalf.

TDPS has licensed Siemens' 2-pole technology for over a decade, so this is that relationship getting upgraded from "we borrow your design" to "we are your factory."

Business only comes through individual purchase orders whenever Siemens issues them. So nothing goes into the order book today, and since these machines take 18–20 months to build, real revenue starts showing up around FY29.

Also, since TDPS is building to Siemens' design and not its own, it doesn't own the technology and likely earns a thinner margin per unit but with far higher volume, less design risk and better factory utilisation.

Think of it as TDPS becoming a "CDMO for generators" for one of the world's top three turbine makers: strategically a very strong position, but for now it's a licence to receive orders, not the orders themselves.

Disclaimer: No recommendation to buy or sell.

China's population is shrinking. Its property sector has collapsed, and taken local government finances down with it. Prices at the factory gate have been falling for years. By most conventional measures, the Chinese economy is in real trouble. And yet, last October, China made a change to its rare-earth export licensing, which sent countries scampering to think about economic statecraft. How does a weakening economy end up with more leverage than ever?

In this episode of Turbulence, Anupam Manur (@anupammanur) is joined by Manoj Kewalramani (@theChinaDude), who chairs the Indo-Pacific Studies Programme at the Takshashila Institution, writes a daily newsletter tracking the Communist Party's own People's Daily, and is the editor of Taming the Dragon: A Manifesto for a New Modus Vivendi with China. The conversation traces China's domestic slowdown, how Beijing exports its overcapacity through outward investment and green tech, what its rare-earth and critical-mineral controls are actually built to do, and how China has quietly de-risked its own economy from the US since 2018.

items.title: RT ANI: #WATCH | Delhi: On the impact of the US tariff bill on the Indian economy, Chief Rating Officer at CareEdge Ratings, Sachin Gupta, says, “It ...
items.description_html:
RT ANI
#WATCH | Delhi: On the impact of the US tariff bill on the Indian economy, Chief Rating Officer at CareEdge Ratings, Sachin Gupta, says, “It will have a multi-order impact on the Indian economy. First of all, we have yet to see how the US implements it, because there is a lot of back-and-forth that happens with many of these US regulations. But assuming that there is indeed a 100% tariff levied, we can analyse this impact at two or three levels. One is the most direct impact, which will be on US imports or Indian exports…if there is indeed a 100% tariff, it becomes unviable…if Russian crude oil supply is excluded from the overall global crude market, where total global crude demand is around 100 million barrels a day, with the Strait of Hormuz accounting for 20 million barrels and Russia accounting for about 9 million barrels, of which India and China take roughly 75% and if both India and China decide not to import from Russia at all due to these 100% tariffs, removing up to 30% of global supply will cause a significant impact. While crude prices have recently been relatively benign at around $70 to $85 a barrel, if this scenario becomes a reality, prices could easily go beyond $100 or even $110 to $120 a barrel, causing India's current account deficit to easily more than double from last year's levels strictly on account of crude. Furthermore, at $110 to $120 a barrel, the government would have to pass on those price rises to the fuel pumps, creating a secondary inflationary impact across the broader economy…”

Forging & casting companies are showing standout growth rates right now.

Take Happy Forgings as an example: 25%+ topline growth and ~40% PAT growth this quarter. Here's why:

This was the fourth straight quarter of 30%+ EBITDA margins and management expects a further 100-150 bps upside as captive power comes online in Q4.

The order book is tilting toward export industrials and PV. A ₹950 crore peak annual revenue pipeline and mostly export-oriented industrial and passenger-vehicle programs is already ramping up and will reshape the revenue mix over the next 2-3 years.

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.description_html:
We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025.

But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea.

> First key factor we observed was the product mix change, where the company's intent was to gradually move from its ICE component business to Aero/Defence/Semicon (ADS) business.

> This product mix shift was visible from the fact that margins had been improving over the last 2 quarters, and growth was starting to pick up. That's how it came under our filters.

> Going a little deeper, we understood that the kind of things it was doing in the ADS business were quite moated. It had a single-source monopoly on Airbus A350/A320 thrust-reversal gimbals with zero defects over 12 years; hogging (machining from solid billet vs. forging) is a much harder-to-replicate capability for aerospace tolerances.

> Also, in its semiconductor business, it was working with Lam Research, where this year their business is expected to go from $10M to $30M .

> Also, as per our channel checks, they had orders/interest from Rolls-Royce for aero-engine feelers, the MMRFIC JV (navy fuses, radars), and a Tesla ESS order.

> All these things were a confirmation of our thesis that management has the capabilities, and that the product mix is changing for good.

> They have also given strong guidance of ₹8,000 Cr in revenue, with ADS at 20–25% of overall business and blended EBITDA margins moving above the 20% mark.

On top of this, we also visited their facility, where we got to understand the manufacturing complexity involved in the components they make for their ADS business, and their capabilities in precision engineering.

The framework was simple: through scanning, found a business where earnings were breaking out and margins were improving > went through their earnings calls and found the story of the product mix change > mapped out the value chain and tried to understand Sansera's moat in the new business they were focusing on > visited their facility to verify our thesis on the company.

Disclaimer: This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. We continue to hold it in our recommendation portfolio and may change our view at any point in time.

items.title: An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works! You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either f...
items.description_html:
An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works!

You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either from a plant you own (merchant) or from a plant you build inside a customer's factory (on-site).

On-site is a 15-20 year annuity at thin margins. A merchant is a spot market where the same molecule earns very different money depending on the gas, the distance, and who else is selling nearby.

The whole game is capital, location, and the ability to squeeze extra high-margin gas (argon, liquid) out of a plant you've already built.

But let’s get into interesting details about that -

What does the industry actually sell?

Strip away the chemistry and this is an air-separation business. A cryogenic plant is an Air Separation Unit, or ASU that chills atmospheric air until its components liquefy at their different boiling points, and pipes off oxygen, nitrogen and argon at high purity. Everyone in the industry runs broadly the same technology, so purity differences are marginal (roughly plus-or-minus 5%). The molecule is a commodity. Almost everything interesting happens around the molecule in how it's contracted, delivered, and priced.

The demand base has historically been the heavy stuff: steel and metals, autos, pharma, healthcare, and a thin slice of chemicals and F&B. What's changing the growth story is the sunrise demand from solar and semiconductors, which pull large volumes of nitrogen and, in semis, demand purity that cheaper suppliers struggle to hit. That single shift is why every player in the country is pouring capital into new capacity at the same time.

The top four global MNCs Linde, INOX Air Products, Air Water India and Air Liquide India control roughly 80% of the market.

Below them sit regional, owner-driven players (Ellenbarrie, Vayu, Shree Ram Oxygas and similar) who have been around 10–15 years and whose space widened after COVID, when oxygen subsidies pulled local capital in.

Now let’s understand the 2 engines in this industry separately > on-site vs merchant

Everything downstream flows from one fork in the road: do you build the plant inside the customer's factory, or near a cluster of customers and truck the gas out? These are two genuinely different businesses with different economics, different customers, and different personalities.

> On-site - An anchor customer, usually a large steel plant, issues an RFQ saying, in effect, we need ~1,100–1,800 tonnes of gas a day flowing into our furnace. A supplier builds and operates an ASU on their premises under a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) contract running 15–20 years. The revenue is fixed and stable, so it's underwritten on a modest return — players will accept an operating margin of roughly 10–12%, sometimes pricing the whole thing to a ~10–15% IRR. It is deliberately boring money.

Why fight so hard for boring money? Because it's stable, long-dated and defensive with a 15–20 year foothold that also keeps a rival out of that customer. Contracts signed before roughly 2016–18 carried fatter margins and some still run (a few end around 2035), but the new-build market is now openly competitive on price.

> Merchant business - Here you own the plant, liquefy the output, and sell it as liquid, bulk or cylinders to whoever's within reach. Margins are structurally better but volatile: liquid/bulk runs a ~20–25% bottom line, while cylinder and specialty can reach ~40%. The catch is geography. Oxygen and nitrogen are cheap and heavy, so you can't economically truck them much beyond ~200–300 km before distribution cost (typically 10–12% of revenue) eats you alive. You plant an ASU, draw a 200–300 km radius, and fight for that circle.

The reason branded MNCs earn ~40–45% at the top while a strong regional player earns ~35% isn't a secret formula rather it's scale and mix. A Linde or INOX moves 4,000–5,000 TPD daily; a regional player moves 250–300 TPD. At a small scale, tender-driven medical demand keeps margins decent. But to scale from 300 TPD to 3,000–4,000 TPD you must chase the lower-margin sectors that make up the bulk of the market and that's exactly where pricing and margin pressure begin.

The value chain, end to end

Follow a molecule of oxygen from the atmosphere to the customer and you can see where value is captured and where it leaks.

Stage 1 - Build the plant (the capital gate)
This is a capital-intensive, power-intensive industry, and the entry cost is the first moat. A modest 200–250 TPD on-site plant needs at least INR 300–400 crore of initial capex. Core components are compressors, cold boxes that have to be imported; India makes none of them. Only fabrication and storage tanks (INOX, Cryolor, VRV) are domestic. Build time runs 16–24 months per ASU

Stage 2 - Choose your engineering partner (the quiet moat)
Who actually builds the plant is becoming the real differentiator. The MNCs carry in-house EPC muscle - Linde has Linde Engineering, INOX leans on Air Products' US technology which lets them build large, reliable ASUs and win the technically demanding jobs.
Regional players without that engineering wing increasingly tie up with Chinese OEMs on a sale-of-equipment basis: the Chinese firm builds and exits, and the local player does the O&M. It's cheaper (a 200 TPD plant runs ~INR 100–120 crore via a Chinese vendor vs ~INR 150–200 crore via an MNC), but blue-chip steelmakers (Tata, JSW, SAIL, AM/NS) often won't allow a Chinese machine where they're underwriting 15–20 years of reliability, power efficiency and capital backup, and they pay up for it.

The cost-vs-capability gap
> MNC plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 150–200 crore — technology, reliability, blue-chip acceptance.
> Chinese plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 100–120 crore — cost-optimised, favoured by smaller / secondary steel and rolling mills.
> No Indian regulation restricts Chinese ASUs, so the split is driven purely by which customer is buying.

Stage 3 - Extract the by-products (where margin hides)
A basic ASU makes oxygen and nitrogen. To pull argon you must bolt on a separate argon-recovery column and here's the quirk: that column costs roughly the same whether the plant is small or large, but a small 200 TPD ASU yields only ~5–6 TPD of argon while a big ASU yields 50–60 TPD. The capital-to-recovery maths favours scale heavily, yet argon's economics are so attractive that even smaller players are now installing the column anyway.

Stage 4 - Distribute (the tyranny of distance)
Oxygen and nitrogen are regional products which are heavy, cheap, and uneconomic beyond ~300 km. Argon is a national product valuable enough to ship across the country, though distribution then runs ~17–18% of revenue rather than 10–12%. This distinction quietly shapes the entire competitive map: oxygen/nitrogen competition is local and radius-bound, while argon competition is national and cyclical.

How to judge any player in this industry?
Pulling the mechanics together, a handful of questions separate a structurally strong operator from a fragile one regardless of the name on the door.

> Capacity trajectory: Can they actually double liquid capacity? You can't sell a molecule if you can't make expansion of 200 TPD takes 1.5 - 2 years, not six months.

> Mix quality: How much on-site annuity vs volatile merchant? How much argon and by-product upside are they extracting per plant?

> Engineering independence: In-house EPC, or dependent on Chinese OEMs who build and exit? This gates which customers they can win.

> Geographic competition: Are their plants in pockets with few rivals inside the 300 km radius, or in contested western/central India?

> Blue-chip acceptance: Can they clear the reliability/purity bar for Tata, JSW, AM/NS, and semiconductors or are they confined to secondary, cost-driven demand?

> Cycle timing: Are they adding capacity into the current glut, and can their balance sheet and geography absorb 2–3 years of merchant price erosion before demand catches up?

Dislaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.description_html:
RT Sagar Awatade
I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here.

Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the last few months have been harder than usual.

We are a small Indian company. For more than ten years we have been building a homegrown brand in a product category dominated by big foreign players.

There are almost no Indian names in this space. We set out to be one.

We started in 2014. Over the years we began making parts in India instead of just importing, and we started selling in the US, Dubai, Nepal, Malaysia and South Africa.

We showed up at global trade fairs to represent an Indian brand on the world stage.

In 2023 we changed the import code we use for our product. We did not do this quietly. Every shipment was declared. Nothing was hidden. We didn't invent our approach.

We followed written professional advice and the way this product is treated in markets around the world.

And now we are facing a government demand running into tens of crores in duty recovery and penalties, plus personal penalties on the founders and even on an employee.

For a company our size, this is not a fine we can pay and move on from. This ends us.

We have not run from any of this. I am not built like that. It is not how I was raised. We have written to the authorities, met officials in person, and we have now filed a writ in the High Court.

All we are asking for is a fair treatment.

I set out to build in India and sell to the world. I am asking only that the system back honest founders trying to compete globally, instead of breaking them.

The process is the process, and it exists for a reason. But process should not feel like punishment.

From where I am standing today, it does.
I am not giving up. I have worked too hard for this. If you have read this far, please share it. If you know someone who can help, point them my way. Help me get the word out.

items.description_html: Agentic routing is such an interesting study. Built a basic agent that does planning on Opus 4 but reasons on 4.6 through a tool call (skill call). Due to lack of document grounding, I embedded corpus into system prompt. Worked well. Second stage, enabled managed RAG for grounding & agent stated skipping tool call entirely, no skill calls. Agent skipped grounding, entered planning mode & made a tool call. Evals for Agentic behavior is literally out paces everything in this field. What's your such key learning from a recent build?
